questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in capital letters: The chairman’s remarks were TERSE.
questions.explanation: “Terse” means brief and abrupt — saying much in few words.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in capital letters: The policy had a DETRIMENTAL effect on trade.
questions.explanation: “Detrimental” means harmful, so its opposite is “beneficial”.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Complete the sentence: If he ______ earlier, he would have caught the bus.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: “if + past perfect” pairs with “would have + past participle”.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the word whose underlined vowel sound is different from the others.
questions.explanation: “Bread” has the short /e/ sound; the others use the long /iː/ sound.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the correct option: Each of the students ______ a copy of the syllabus.
questions.explanation: “Each” is singular, so it takes the singular verb “has”.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: In the sentence “The meeting was called off”, the expression “called off” means the meeting was
questions.explanation: To “call off” something is to cancel it.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Choose the option that best completes the sentence: The manager insisted that every worker ______ present at the briefing.
questions.explanation: After “insist that” the subjunctive is used, so the base form “be” is correct.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: In not more than 60 words, explain the difference between a formal and an informal letter, and give one situation in which each is appropriate.
questions.expected: A formal letter uses an impersonal, respectful tone, avoids contractions and slang, and carries both the writer’s and the recipient’s addresses with a formal salutation and closing — appropriate for official matters such as a job application. An informal letter is personal and conversational, allows contractions, and carries only the writer’s address — appropriate for writing to a friend or relative.

questions.subject: Use of English
questions.text: Write a topic sentence for a paragraph arguing that reading widely improves writing, then give two supporting points.
questions.expected: A suitable topic sentence states the claim clearly, e.g. “Wide reading is the surest way to become a better writer.” Supporting points may include: exposure to varied sentence patterns and vocabulary that the writer then reuses; and familiarity with how ideas are organised and paragraphs are linked, which improves the writer’s own structure. Award marks for a clear topic sentence (4) and two relevant, developed points (3 each).

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Simplify $(2^3 \times 2^5) \div 2^4$.
questions.explanation: Add the indices when multiplying and subtract when dividing: $3 + 5 - 4 = 4$, so the answer is $2^4$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: If $3x - 7 = 11$, find $x$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon.
questions.explanation: The sum of the interior angles is $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$, so for a hexagon $(6 - 2) \times 180^\circ = 720^\circ$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: The mean of 4, 7, $x$ and 10 is 8. Find $x$.
questions.explanation: The total must be $4 \times 8 = 32$. Since $4 + 7 + 10 = 21$, $x = 32 - 21 = 11$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Find the gradient of the straight line joining the points $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 11)$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: Evaluate $\log_{10} 8 + \log_{10} 125$.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.text: The 3rd term of an arithmetic progression is 11 and the 7th term is 27. Find the common difference.
questions.explanation: Four steps separate the 3rd and 7th terms, so $4d = 27 - 11 = 16$ and $d = 4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The SI unit of electric charge is the
questions.explanation: Charge is measured in coulombs; the ampere measures current, the volt potential difference and the ohm resistance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A body starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $4\ \text{m/s}^2$ for 5 seconds. Find its final velocity.
questions.explanation: $v = u + at = 0 + (4 \times 5) = 20\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Momentum has both magnitude and direction; the others are scalars.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Convert 27 °C to kelvin.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz and a wavelength of 4 m. Calculate its speed.
questions.explanation: $v = f\lambda = 50 \times 4 = 200\ \text{m/s}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A transformer has 200 turns in the primary coil and 1,000 in the secondary. If the primary voltage is 40 V, the secondary voltage is
questions.explanation: $\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = 5$, so $V_s = 40 \times 5 = 200\ \text{V}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A machine with a velocity ratio of 5 has an efficiency of 80%. Find its mechanical advantage.
questions.explanation: Efficiency $= \frac{MA}{VR}$, so $MA = 0.8 \times 5 = 4$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: State Ohm’s law and explain one condition under which it does not hold.
questions.expected: Ohm’s law: the current flowing through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends, provided temperature and other physical conditions remain constant. It fails when the temperature of the conductor changes appreciably, and it does not apply to non-ohmic devices such as filament lamps, semiconductor diodes, gases and electrolytes. Award marks for a correct statement including the constant-conditions proviso (6) and one valid limitation (4).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A stone is thrown vertically upwards with a velocity of 20 m/s. Taking $g = 10\ \text{m/s}^2$, calculate the maximum height reached and the total time of flight.
questions.expected: At maximum height the final velocity is zero, so $h = \frac{u^2}{2g} = \frac{400}{20} = 20\ \text{m}$. Time to reach the top $= \frac{u}{g} = \frac{20}{10} = 2\ \text{s}$, and since the motion is symmetrical the total time of flight is 4 s. Award marks for the height with working (5) and the total time (5).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: The general molecular formula of alkanes is
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with the general formula $C_nH_{2n+2}$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of a physical change?
questions.explanation: Melting is reversible and forms no new substance, so it is a physical change.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: How many moles are present in 44 g of carbon(IV) oxide? [C = 12, O = 16]
questions.explanation: The molar mass of $CO_2$ is $12 + 32 = 44$ g/mol, so $n = \frac{44}{44} = 1$ mole.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: During electrolysis, oxidation takes place at the
questions.explanation: Anions migrate to the anode and lose electrons, so oxidation occurs there.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: A solution with a pH of 3 is
questions.explanation: A pH below 7 is acidic; pH 3 indicates a fairly strong acid.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Which gas turns lime water milky?
questions.explanation: Carbon(IV) oxide forms insoluble calcium trioxocarbonate(IV) with lime water, giving the milky appearance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: What is the oxidation number of manganese in $KMnO_4$?
questions.explanation: Potassium is $+1$ and each oxygen is $-2$, giving $1 + x - 8 = 0$, so $x = +7$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Define electrolysis and state two industrial applications of it.
questions.expected: Electrolysis is the decomposition of an electrolyte by the passage of an electric current through it in the molten or aqueous state. Industrial applications include: electroplating of metals; the extraction of reactive metals such as aluminium and sodium from their molten ores; the refining or purification of copper; and the manufacture of chlorine and sodium hydroxide from brine. Award marks for the definition (4) and two valid applications (3 each).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.text: Explain, with an equation, why alkanes undergo substitution rather than addition reactions with chlorine.
questions.expected: Alkanes are saturated: every carbon atom is joined by single covalent bonds and already holds the maximum number of hydrogen atoms, so there is no double or triple bond for a reagent to add across. Chlorine therefore replaces a hydrogen atom instead. In the presence of sunlight: $CH_4 + Cl_2 \to CH_3Cl + HCl$. Award marks for the explanation based on saturation (6) and a correct balanced equation (4).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The basic structural and functional unit of life is the
questions.explanation: All living things are built from cells, which are the smallest units able to carry out life processes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which organelle is the site of photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which traps the light energy used in photosynthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: The blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart is the
questions.explanation: The pulmonary vein is the exception among veins: it carries oxygenated blood, from the lungs to the left atrium.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: In humans, the sex chromosomes of a normal male are
questions.explanation: Males carry one X and one Y chromosome; females carry two X chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Which of the following is an excretory organ in mammals?
questions.explanation: The kidneys remove urea, excess water and salts from the blood as urine.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Organisms that manufacture their own food from simple inorganic substances are called
questions.explanation: Producers, mainly green plants, are autotrophic and form the first trophic level.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: A cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt) gives a phenotypic ratio of
questions.explanation: The offspring are TT, Tt, Tt and tt — three tall to one short, a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: Define photosynthesis and write the balanced overall equation for the process.
questions.expected: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy trapped by chlorophyll to convert carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrate, releasing oxygen as a by-product. Overall equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, in the presence of light and chlorophyll. Award marks for a definition mentioning light energy, chlorophyll and the raw materials (6) and a correctly balanced equation (4).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.text: State three differences between arteries and veins.
questions.expected: Any three of the following: arteries carry blood away from the heart while veins carry blood towards it; arteries carry oxygenated blood (except the pulmonary artery) while veins carry deoxygenated blood (except the pulmonary vein); arteries have thick muscular elastic walls and a narrow lumen while veins have thin walls and a wide lumen; veins contain valves to prevent backflow while arteries do not; blood in arteries is under high pressure and flows in spurts, whereas blood in veins is under low pressure and flows smoothly. Award 3 marks per valid, clearly stated difference.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
notes.body:
A verb must agree with its subject in number: a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. The difficulty is finding the real subject, because words often sit between it and the verb.

In "the box of pencils is on the table", the subject is "box", not "pencils" — the phrase "of pencils" does not change the number.

Subjects joined by "and" are plural, but subjects joined by "or", "either...or" or "neither...nor" agree with the part nearest the verb. Words like everyone, each, nobody and somebody are singular, however plural they feel.

Exam tip: read past the words between the subject and the verb before you choose.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Reading for the Nearest Meaning
notes.body:
Lexis questions ask for the option nearest in meaning to a word as it is used in the sentence, not its dictionary meaning in general. The sentence is the evidence.

Work in three steps. First read the whole sentence and decide whether the word is positive, negative or neutral. Second, eliminate the options that carry the wrong feeling. Third, test the remaining options by substituting each one into the sentence.

Exam tip: an option that is a synonym in some other context is the commonest trap. Substitution catches it.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: Quadratic Equations
notes.body:
A quadratic equation has the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, where $a$ is not zero. You can solve it by factorising, by completing the square, or with the quadratic formula, which always works:

$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$

The part under the root, $b^2 - 4ac$, is the discriminant. If it is positive there are two distinct real roots; if it is zero the roots are equal; if it is negative there are no real roots.

Exam tip: try factorising first. It is faster than the formula when the numbers are small, and most examination questions are built to factorise.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: The Laws of Indices
notes.body:
Indices are a shorthand for repeated multiplication, and every rule follows from that. Multiplying powers of the same base adds the indices, $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$; dividing subtracts them, $a^m \div a^n = a^{m-n}$; raising a power to a power multiplies them, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$.

Two special cases are worth memorising because they are tested constantly. Any non-zero number to the power zero is 1, so $a^0 = 1$. A negative index means a reciprocal, so $2^{-3} = \frac{1}{8}$. A fractional index is a root: $8^{\frac{1}{3}} = 2$.

Exam tip: write every number in the question to the same base before you start. Most index questions collapse in one line once you do.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Acceleration
notes.body:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time. It is a vector, so it has both a size and a direction: an object slowing down is still accelerating, just in the direction opposite to its motion.

For uniform acceleration, $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$, where $u$ is the initial velocity, $v$ the final velocity and $t$ the time taken. The SI unit is the metre per second squared, $\text{m/s}^2$.

On a velocity-time graph, the acceleration is the gradient of the line and the area under the line is the distance travelled.

Exam tip: check the units before you calculate. A velocity given in km/h must be divided by 3.6 to become m/s.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Ohm’s Law
notes.body:
Ohm’s law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature stays constant. In symbols, $V = IR$.

In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere and the resistances add, $R = R_1 + R_2$. In a parallel circuit the potential difference is the same across each branch, and the reciprocals of the resistances add: $\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$.

Exam tip: redraw the circuit before you calculate. Most mistakes in this topic are mistakes about which components are in series and which are in parallel, not about arithmetic.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Alkanes
notes.body:
Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons: they contain only carbon and hydrogen joined by single covalent bonds. Because every carbon carries as many hydrogen atoms as possible, they are described as saturated.

Their general formula is $C_nH_{2n+2}$, which lets you work out any member. When $n = 1$ you get methane, $CH_4$; when $n = 2$ you get ethane, $C_2H_6$; when $n = 3$, propane, $C_3H_8$.

Alkanes are generally unreactive, but they burn in air and undergo substitution reactions with halogens in the presence of sunlight.

Exam tip: memorise the first four names in order — methane, ethane, propane, butane.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Moles and the Avogadro Constant
notes.body:
A mole is an amount of substance containing as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12: $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles, the Avogadro constant.

Three relationships do most of the work. Number of moles equals mass divided by molar mass, $n = \frac{m}{M}$. Number of moles equals number of particles divided by the Avogadro constant, $n = \frac{N}{N_A}$. For a gas at s.t.p., number of moles equals volume divided by $22.4\ \text{dm}^3$.

Exam tip: write down which of the three you have been given before choosing a formula. Nearly every mole calculation is one of these three, or two of them joined by a balanced equation.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: The Cell as a Unit of Life
notes.body:
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of all living things. Plant and animal cells share a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane, but a plant cell also has a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.

The nucleus holds the chromosomes and controls the activities of the cell. The mitochondrion releases energy from food in respiration, which is why hard-working cells such as muscle and liver cells contain very many of them.

Exam tip: questions often turn on a single difference. Chloroplasts and a cellulose wall are plant only; centrioles are animal only.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Photosynthesis
notes.body:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by chlorophyll, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

It happens in two stages. The light stage splits water and stores energy; the dark stage uses that energy to fix carbon dioxide into sugar. The rate is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply — light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.

Exam tip: a graph in this topic is almost always about a limiting factor. Look for where the curve levels off and ask what has run short.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Synonyms and Antonyms: A Working Method
notes.body:
Synonym and antonym questions are not a vocabulary guessing game — they test whether you can read a word the way it is used in the sentence, not just its dictionary meaning in isolation.

Start by deciding the "feeling" of the underlined word: is it positive, negative, or neutral in that sentence? This single step eliminates half the options immediately, because wrong answers are often built from words with the opposite feeling.

Next, substitute your remaining candidates directly into the sentence. The correct synonym should sound natural in that exact context; a word can be a synonym in one sentence and completely wrong in another. For antonyms, apply the same substitution test but look for the option that reverses the sentence's meaning most precisely, not just any vaguely "opposite" word.

Exam tip: many wrong options are a synonym or antonym of a different, related word in the sentence — read narrowly, and always trust the sentence over your first instinct.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Reading Comprehension: Working the Passage, Not Your Memory
notes.body:
Comprehension questions punish candidates who rely on memory of similar topics instead of what the passage actually says. Every correct answer must be traceable back to a specific line or idea in the text.

Read the passage once fully before looking at the questions, noting the writer's overall attitude (is it critical, sympathetic, neutral?) and the structure (does it compare two things, argue a case, or simply describe?). Then read each question and go back to locate the exact section it is testing — most answers sit within one or two sentences of the passage.

Be especially careful with inference questions ("What can be inferred...", "The passage suggests..."). These are not asking for a direct quote but for the one conclusion the passage's own evidence supports — reject any option that requires outside knowledge not given in the passage, however true it may be in real life.

Exam tip: when two options both seem partly correct, choose the one that uses the passage's own reasoning, not the one that simply sounds more sophisticated.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Subject–Verb Agreement in Tricky Structures
notes.body:
Most concord mistakes happen not with simple sentences but with structures that hide the true subject: phrases with "as well as," "together with," "along with," and "in addition to" do NOT make the subject plural — the verb agrees only with the main subject named first.

Indefinite pronouns such as each, everybody, nobody, someone, anyone, and either are always singular, however plural they feel in meaning. "Each of the students has a locker" is correct, not "have."

Correlative conjunctions behave differently: "either...or" and "neither...nor" make the verb agree with the noun closest to it — "Neither the manager nor his assistants were available" is correct because "assistants" (plural) is nearer the verb.

Collective nouns (team, committee, jury, family) usually take a singular verb when acting as one unit, but can take a plural verb when members are considered as individuals acting separately — "The jury were divided in their opinions."

Exam tip: physically cross out the interrupting phrase between the subject and the verb before deciding which verb form fits.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Direct and Indirect Speech: The Three Shifts
notes.body:
Converting direct speech to reported (indirect) speech in JAMB always tests the same three changes together, and missing any one of them is what turns a correct answer into a wrong one.

First, the tense shifts one step back into the past: present simple becomes past simple, present continuous becomes past continuous, present perfect becomes past perfect, and simple future ("will") becomes "would." Second, pronouns change to match the speaker's new perspective — "I" often becomes "he" or "she," and "my" becomes "his" or "her." Third, time and place expressions shift: "now" becomes "then," "today" becomes "that day," "tomorrow" becomes "the next/following day," and "here" becomes "there."

Reported questions have an extra rule: the word order returns to normal statement order (no inversion), and no question mark is used — "She asked where I was going," not "She asked where was I going."

Exam tip: rewrite the sentence one shift at a time — tense first, then pronouns, then time/place words — rather than trying to change everything in your head at once.

notes.subject: Use of English
notes.title: Understanding Idioms Without Memorising Hundreds
notes.body:
JAMB idiom questions cannot realistically be prepared for by memorising an endless list — instead, learn idioms in family groups built around a shared image, which makes the meaning easier to recall under exam pressure.

Idioms about difficulty or hardship often use physical struggle as their image: "bite the bullet" (endure something painful), "face the music" (accept unpleasant consequences), and "an uphill task" (something very difficult) all share this pattern.

Idioms about secrecy or revelation often use containers or hidden objects: "let the cat out of the bag" (reveal a secret), "spill the beans" (also reveal a secret), and "skeletons in the closet" (hidden shameful facts).

Idioms about agreement or disagreement often use physical position: "on the same page" (agreeing), "see eye to eye" (agreeing), and "at loggerheads" (in serious disagreement).

Exam tip: when unsure, read the idiom literally first — many idioms retain a trace of their literal image, which often points you toward the figurative meaning being tested.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: Solving Simultaneous Linear Equations
notes.body:
Simultaneous equations ask you to find values that satisfy two (or more) equations at once. JAMB almost always uses linear pairs, solvable by either substitution or elimination.

In the elimination method, you make the coefficient of one variable identical in both equations (by multiplying one or both equations), then add or subtract the equations to remove that variable. For example, to solve $2x + y = 8$ and $x - y = 1$, adding the two equations directly eliminates $y$: $3x = 9$, so $x = 3$, and substituting back gives $y = 2$.

In the substitution method, you make one variable the subject of one equation and substitute it into the other. This is often faster when one equation already has a variable with a coefficient of 1, as in $x - y = 1 \Rightarrow x = y + 1$.

For simultaneous equations where one is linear and one is quadratic, always substitute the linear equation into the quadratic one — this reduces the system to a single quadratic equation in one variable, which you then solve normally and substitute back for the other variable.

Exam tip: always check your solution by substituting both values back into the ORIGINAL equations, not just the one you used last — this catches sign errors instantly.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: Trigonometric Ratios and Standard Angles
notes.body:
Trigonometry in JAMB is built almost entirely on right-angled triangles and a small set of standard angle values that you must know instantly, without a calculator.

The three basic ratios are defined relative to a chosen angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle: $\sin\theta = \frac{opposite}{hypotenuse}$, $\cos\theta = \frac{adjacent}{hypotenuse}$, and $\tan\theta = \frac{opposite}{adjacent}$. A useful memory aid is "SOH-CAH-TOA."

You must memorise these standard values: $\sin 30° = \frac{1}{2}$, $\cos 30° = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\sin 45° = \cos 45° = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, $\sin 60° = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\cos 60° = \frac{1}{2}$, and $\tan 45° = 1$. Also remember that $\sin 90° = 1$ and $\cos 0° = 1$.

The 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 triangles come up repeatedly in "find sin θ given tan θ" style questions — if $\tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}$, the hypotenuse is 5 (by Pythagoras), so $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\cos\theta = \frac{4}{5}$ without any further calculation.

Exam tip: for angle-of-elevation/depression word problems, always sketch the right-angled triangle first — most errors come from misplacing which side is "opposite" and which is "adjacent."

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: Differentiation: The Basic Rules
notes.body:
Differentiation finds the rate of change of a function — practically, the gradient of a curve at a specific point. JAMB tests only the basic polynomial rule and its direct applications.

The core rule: for a term $ax^n$, the derivative is $anx^{n-1}$ — multiply by the power, then reduce the power by one. Applied term by term, if $y = 3x^2 + 2x - 5$, then $\frac{dy}{dx} = 6x + 2$ (the constant $-5$ disappears because the derivative of any constant is zero).

To find the gradient of a curve at a specific point, differentiate the function, then substitute the given $x$-value into the derivative — never into the original equation for this purpose.

Differentiation also gives velocity and acceleration from a displacement function: if $s$ is displacement in terms of time $t$, then velocity $v = \frac{ds}{dt}$ and acceleration $a = \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{d^2s}{dt^2}$. So for $s = t^3 - 2t$, velocity is $v = 3t^2 - 2$, and at $t = 2$, $v = 3(4) - 2 = 10$.

Exam tip: watch for questions asking for a "stationary point" or "turning point" — these occur where $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$; set the derivative equal to zero and solve for $x$.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: Sets: Notation, Operations, and the Venn Diagram Formula
notes.body:
Set questions in JAMB revolve around a small number of symbols and one key formula that must be memorised exactly.

Union ($A \cup B$) means everything in A, in B, or in both. Intersection ($A \cap B$) means only what is common to both A and B. The complement ($A'$) means everything in the universal set that is NOT in A.

The most tested formula is: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. This corrects for double-counting the overlap. For three sets, students only pushed to describe overlaps carefully using a Venn diagram — sketching the diagram and filling numbers from the innermost overlap outward avoids almost all careless errors.

For word problems ("30 students offer Maths, 25 offer Physics, 10 offer both, how many offer neither out of 50?"), always compute $n(A \cup B)$ first using the formula above, then subtract from the total to find "neither."

Exam tip: when a Venn diagram problem gives you the number in an overlap region directly, place that number first before filling in the rest of the diagram — it anchors every other calculation.

notes.subject: Mathematics
notes.title: Indices, Logarithms and Surds: The Shared Rules
notes.body:
Indices, logarithms, and surds are frequently tested together because they share underlying laws that, once learned, apply across all three.

Laws of indices: $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$, $a^m \div a^n = a^{m-n}$, $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$, $a^0 = 1$, and $a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n}$. A fractional index represents a root: $a^{\frac{1}{n}} = \sqrt[n]{a}$.

Logarithms are the inverse of indices: if $a^x = y$, then $\log_a y = x$. The key log laws are $\log(mn) = \log m + \log n$, $\log\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) = \log m - \log n$, and $\log(m^n) = n\log m$.

Surds are irrational roots left in root form (e.g. $\sqrt{2}$). To simplify a surd, extract the largest perfect-square factor: $\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25 \times 2} = 5\sqrt{2}$. To rationalise a denominator like $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, multiply top and bottom by $\sqrt{3}$ to get $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$.

Exam tip: for number-base conversion questions, remember each digit's place value is a power of the base counted from the right, starting at power zero — this is the fastest way to convert any base to base 10.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
notes.body:
Newton's three laws form the foundation of almost every mechanics question in JAMB Physics, and each has a distinct, testable idea.

The first law (law of inertia) states that a body remains at rest, or in uniform motion in a straight line, unless acted upon by a resultant external force. This explains why passengers lurch forward when a moving vehicle suddenly stops — their bodies continue moving due to inertia.

The second law is the most calculation-heavy: the resultant force on a body equals the rate of change of momentum, commonly simplified to $F = ma$ (force equals mass times acceleration) when mass is constant. This single formula underlies most "find the acceleration/force/mass" questions.

The third law states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. These two forces act on DIFFERENT objects, not the same one — this is the detail JAMB most often tests, since a common wrong answer treats action and reaction as cancelling out on the same body.

Exam tip: in $F = ma$ problems, always check that all quantities are in SI units (kilograms, metres, seconds) before substituting — a mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms first.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Ohm's Law and Resistor Combinations
notes.body:
Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, provided temperature remains constant: $V = IR$, where $V$ is voltage in volts, $I$ is current in amperes, and $R$ is resistance in ohms.

For resistors in series, the total resistance is simply the sum of individual resistances: $R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3$. The same current flows through every resistor in a series circuit, but the voltage divides across them.

For resistors in parallel, the reciprocal of the total resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of each resistance: $\frac{1}{R_{total}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}$. In a parallel circuit, the voltage across each resistor is the same, but the current divides between the branches. Note that the total resistance in a parallel arrangement is always LESS than the smallest individual resistance — a common way JAMB checks whether you truly understand the concept rather than just plugging into a formula.

Electrical power can be calculated as $P = IV = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$, and energy consumed is $E = Pt$, often expressed in kilowatt-hours (kWh) for billing purposes.

Exam tip: for parallel resistor questions, if only two resistors are given, use the shortcut $R_{total} = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ instead of working with reciprocals — it is faster and less error-prone.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Wave Properties and the Wave Equation
notes.body:
A wave transfers energy from one point to another without transferring matter itself, and JAMB tests both the vocabulary of waves and the core equation linking their properties.

Key terms: wavelength ($\lambda$) is the distance between two successive identical points on a wave (e.g. crest to crest); frequency ($f$) is the number of complete waves passing a point per second, measured in hertz; amplitude is the maximum displacement from the rest position; and period ($T$) is the time taken for one complete wave, related to frequency by $T = \frac{1}{f}$.

The fundamental wave equation connects these: $v = f\lambda$, where $v$ is the speed of the wave. This single formula can answer most numerical wave questions once you identify which two quantities are given.

Waves are classified as transverse (vibrations perpendicular to the direction of travel, like light and water waves) or longitudinal (vibrations parallel to the direction of travel, like sound waves). Only mechanical waves such as sound need a material medium to travel; electromagnetic waves such as light and radio waves can travel through a vacuum.

Exam tip: when a question gives wavelength in centimetres but asks for frequency in hertz using speed in metres per second, always convert wavelength to metres first — unit mismatches are the most common source of wrong numerical answers.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
notes.body:
Specific heat capacity is the quantity of heat energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 Kelvin (or 1°C). The formula is $Q = mc\Delta\theta$, where $Q$ is heat energy in joules, $m$ is mass in kilograms, $c$ is specific heat capacity in J/kgK, and $\Delta\theta$ is the change in temperature.

Different substances have different specific heat capacities — water has an unusually high one (4200 J/kgK), which is why water heats up and cools down more slowly than most other common substances, and why it is used in cooling systems.

Latent heat, by contrast, is the heat energy involved in a CHANGE OF STATE, without any change in temperature. The specific latent heat of fusion is the heat needed to change 1 kg of a solid to liquid at its melting point, while the specific latent heat of vaporisation is the heat needed to change 1 kg of liquid to gas at its boiling point. The formula is simply $Q = mL$, with no temperature term at all, because temperature stays constant during a change of state.

Exam tip: if a problem involves both heating a substance AND changing its state (e.g. heating ice to steam), solve it in separate stages — heating solid, melting, heating liquid, boiling, heating gas — and add the heat energy from each stage.

notes.subject: Physics
notes.title: Reflection and Refraction of Light
notes.body:
Reflection occurs when light bounces off a surface, obeying the law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal (an imaginary line perpendicular to the surface).

Plane mirrors always produce a virtual, upright image that is the same size as the object and appears as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it. Curved mirrors behave differently: a concave mirror can produce either a real, inverted image (when the object is beyond the focal point) or a virtual, magnified image (when the object is between the mirror and the focal point) — the exact image depends on the object's position relative to the focal point and centre of curvature.

Refraction occurs when light passes from one transparent medium to another of different density, causing it to change speed and bend. Light bends TOWARDS the normal when entering a denser medium (e.g. air to glass) and AWAY from the normal when entering a less dense medium (e.g. glass to air).

Total internal reflection happens when light travelling in a denser medium strikes the boundary with a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle — instead of refracting out, all the light reflects back into the denser medium. This principle is used in optical fibres.

Exam tip: for mirror/lens image questions, remember the rule of thumb — "beyond centre of curvature/2F gives a smaller real image; between focal point and mirror/lens gives a bigger virtual image.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: The Periodic Table: Trends Across Periods and Down Groups
notes.body:
The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, and understanding its trends lets you predict properties without memorising every element individually.

Across a period (left to right), atomic radius DECREASES because each added electron enters the same energy level while the increasing number of protons pulls the electron cloud in tighter. Ionisation energy generally INCREASES across a period for the same reason — electrons are held more tightly and require more energy to remove.

Down a group, atomic radius INCREASES because each element down the group has an additional occupied energy level, placing outer electrons further from the nucleus. Ionisation energy DECREASES down a group because outer electrons, being farther from the nucleus and shielded by inner electrons, are more easily removed.

Metallic character increases down a group and decreases across a period from left to right — this is why Group 1 (alkali metals) are the most reactive metals, and elements on the far right (halogens, noble gases) are non-metallic.

Exam tip: elements in the same GROUP (vertical column) have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of valence electrons — this is the single most useful fact for predicting an unfamiliar element's behaviour.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Ionic, Covalent and Metallic Bonding Compared
notes.body:
Chemical bonding explains why atoms join together, and JAMB expects you to distinguish clearly between the three main types.

Ionic bonding occurs between a metal and a non-metal, involving the complete TRANSFER of electrons from the metal (which becomes a positive ion) to the non-metal (which becomes a negative ion). The resulting oppositely charged ions attract each other electrostatically. Ionic compounds, like sodium chloride, typically have high melting points and conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, but not as solids.

Covalent bonding occurs between two non-metals, involving the SHARING of electron pairs so both atoms attain a stable electron configuration. Covalent compounds, like water and carbon dioxide, generally have lower melting points than ionic compounds and do not conduct electricity in any state (with some exceptions).

Metallic bonding occurs between metal atoms, where positive metal ions are held together in a "sea" of delocalised electrons that are free to move throughout the structure. This explains why metals conduct electricity and heat well, and why they are malleable and ductile — the delocalised electrons allow layers of ions to slide past each other without breaking the bond.

Exam tip: if a question asks about a substance's ability to conduct electricity as a solid, it is almost always testing whether you correctly identify metallic or ionic (in solution/molten) bonding — pure covalent solids do not conduct.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: The Mole Concept and Simple Stoichiometry
notes.body:
The mole is the chemist's counting unit, letting us relate the invisible world of atoms and molecules to measurable masses in the laboratory. One mole of any substance contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles (Avogadro's number).

The key formula is: $\text{number of moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}$. So to find how many moles are in 22g of $CO_2$ (molar mass 44 g/mol), divide: $\frac{22}{44} = 0.5$ moles.

Molar mass is calculated by adding the atomic masses of all atoms in the formula — for $CO_2$, that is $12 + (16 \times 2) = 44$ g/mol.

For reacting masses in a balanced equation, the mole ratio (shown by the balancing numbers) tells you how the reactants and products relate. For example, in $N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3$, one mole of nitrogen always reacts with exactly three moles of hydrogen to give two moles of ammonia — this ratio is fixed regardless of the actual quantities used.

Exam tip: always balance the chemical equation FIRST before doing any mole calculation — an unbalanced equation gives the wrong mole ratio and will lead to a wrong final answer, even if your arithmetic is correct.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Acids, Bases and the pH Scale
notes.body:
An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions ($H^+$) in aqueous solution, while a base is a substance that releases hydroxide ions ($OH^-$) or accepts hydrogen ions. A base that dissolves in water is specifically called an alkali.

The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a solution is, ranging from 0 to 14. A pH of 7 is neutral (pure water); values below 7 are acidic, with lower numbers indicating stronger acidity; values above 7 are basic (alkaline), with higher numbers indicating stronger basicity.

Strong acids and bases ionise completely in water (e.g. hydrochloric acid, sodium hydroxide), while weak acids and bases only partially ionise (e.g. ethanoic/acetic acid, ammonia solution) — strength is about the DEGREE of ionisation, not the concentration of the solution.

Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water: $\text{Acid} + \text{Base} \rightarrow \text{Salt} + \text{Water}$. The specific salt formed depends on both the acid used (e.g. sulphuric acid gives sulphate salts, hydrochloric acid gives chloride salts) and the metal or base used.

Exam tip: do not confuse "strong/weak" (degree of ionisation) with "concentrated/dilute" (amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of water) — a dilute solution of a strong acid can still have a very low pH if enough acid is dissolved.

notes.subject: Chemistry
notes.title: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes and Their Reactions
notes.body:
Hydrocarbons are compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen, and JAMB focuses heavily on the two simplest families: alkanes and alkenes.

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, meaning they contain only single carbon-carbon bonds, with the general formula $C_nH_{2n+2}$. They are relatively unreactive and mainly undergo combustion (burning in oxygen to give carbon dioxide and water) and substitution reactions (e.g. reacting with halogens under UV light, where a hydrogen atom is replaced by a halogen atom).

Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons, containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond, with the general formula $C_nH_{2n}$. This double bond makes them more reactive than alkanes, readily undergoing addition reactions — for example, reacting with bromine water to decolourise it, a classic test used to distinguish alkenes from alkanes (which do not decolourise bromine water).

Alkenes also undergo addition polymerisation, where many small alkene monomers join together to form a long-chain polymer — ethene monomers combine to form polythene, a process widely used industrially.

Exam tip: "decolourises bromine water" is a signature test question for unsaturation (a double bond) — if a substance decolourises bromine water, it is an alkene (or another unsaturated compound), not an alkane.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Cell Structure: Plant and Animal Cells Compared
notes.body:
All living things are made of cells, the basic structural and functional unit of life, and JAMB frequently tests the differences between plant and animal cells.

Both cell types share key structures: a cell membrane (controls what enters and leaves the cell), cytoplasm (the jelly-like substance where cellular reactions occur), a nucleus (contains genetic material and controls cell activities), mitochondria (the site of aerobic respiration, producing energy), and ribosomes (the site of protein synthesis).

Plant cells possess three additional structures that animal cells lack: a rigid CELL WALL made of cellulose (providing shape and support), a large permanent VACUOLE filled with cell sap (maintaining turgor pressure), and CHLOROPLASTS containing chlorophyll (the site of photosynthesis, found only in green plant parts).

Animal cells, by contrast, often have small, temporary vacuoles (if any), no cell wall (giving them a more flexible, irregular shape), and no chloroplasts, since animals cannot photosynthesise and must obtain food from other organisms.

Exam tip: if a diagram question shows a cell with a distinct rigid outer boundary AND green organelles, it is unmistakably a plant cell — the cell wall and chloroplasts are the two most reliable identifying features.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Photosynthesis: Requirements and the Overall Equation
notes.body:
Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants manufacture their own food (glucose) using light energy, and it is one of the most heavily tested topics in JAMB Biology.

The overall word equation is: carbon dioxide + water $\xrightarrow{\text{light, chlorophyll}}$ glucose + oxygen. The raw materials are carbon dioxide (absorbed through stomata in the leaves) and water (absorbed by roots and transported via the xylem); the products are glucose (used for energy or stored as starch) and oxygen (released as a by-product, mostly through the stomata).

Chlorophyll, the green pigment found in chloroplasts, absorbs light energy (mainly red and blue wavelengths, while reflecting green light — which is why leaves appear green) and converts it into chemical energy used to drive the reaction.

Several factors limit the rate of photosynthesis: light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, and temperature. At any given time, whichever factor is in shortest supply becomes the "limiting factor" that caps the overall rate, regardless of how abundant the other factors are.

Exam tip: a plant deprived of light will still respire (using up stored food) but cannot photosynthesise — this distinction between respiration (occurs at all times) and photosynthesis (requires light) is a common source of confusion in exam questions.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: The Human Circulatory System
notes.body:
The human circulatory system transports blood, and with it oxygen, nutrients, hormones and waste products, around the body via a network of blood vessels driven by the heart.

The heart has four chambers: two upper atria (which receive blood) and two lower ventricles (which pump blood out). The right side of the heart handles deoxygenated blood, receiving it from the body via the right atrium and pumping it to the lungs via the right ventricle. The left side handles oxygenated blood, receiving it from the lungs via the left atrium and pumping it to the rest of the body via the left ventricle — the left ventricle has the thickest, most muscular wall because it must generate enough pressure to pump blood around the entire body.

Three main types of blood vessels exist: arteries (carry blood away from the heart, usually oxygenated, under high pressure, with thick muscular walls), veins (carry blood back to the heart, usually deoxygenated, under lower pressure, with valves to prevent backflow), and capillaries (tiny vessels with walls one cell thick, allowing exchange of substances between blood and body tissues).

Blood itself consists of red blood cells (carry oxygen using haemoglobin), white blood cells (fight infection), platelets (aid clotting), and plasma (the liquid component that transports dissolved substances).

Exam tip: remember the exception to "arteries carry oxygenated blood" — the pulmonary artery carries DEOXYGENATED blood to the lungs, and the pulmonary vein carries OXYGENATED blood back to the heart, the reverse of the usual pattern elsewhere in the body.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Mendelian Inheritance: The Monohybrid Cross
notes.body:
Genetics studies how characteristics are passed from parents to offspring, and JAMB focuses mainly on simple monohybrid crosses based on Gregor Mendel's principles.

Key terms: a GENE is a unit of heredity that controls a characteristic; an ALLELE is a version of a gene (e.g. the allele for tallness or shortness in a pea plant); GENOTYPE is the genetic makeup of an organism (e.g. Tt); PHENOTYPE is the observable physical characteristic resulting from the genotype (e.g. tall); DOMINANT alleles are expressed whenever present (shown with a capital letter), while RECESSIVE alleles are only expressed when no dominant allele is present (shown with a lowercase letter); HOMOZYGOUS means having two identical alleles (TT or tt), while HETEROZYGOUS means having two different alleles (Tt).

In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygous individuals (Tt x Tt), the expected genotypic ratio of offspring is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, which produces a phenotypic ratio of 3 dominant : 1 recessive — this 3:1 ratio is one of the most frequently tested numbers in JAMB genetics.

A cross between a homozygous dominant (TT) and a homozygous recessive (tt) parent produces ALL heterozygous (Tt) offspring, all showing the dominant phenotype, since every offspring receives one dominant and one recessive allele.

Exam tip: always draw a simple Punnett square for cross questions rather than trying to work out ratios mentally — it takes seconds and prevents careless errors in tracking which alleles combine.

notes.subject: Biology
notes.title: Ecosystems, Food Chains and Energy Flow
notes.body:
An ecosystem is a community of living organisms (biotic factors) interacting with their non-living environment (abiotic factors, such as sunlight, temperature, and soil pH) within a defined area.

A food chain shows the linear flow of energy from one organism to another, always starting with a PRODUCER (usually a green plant, which makes its own food via photosynthesis), followed by a PRIMARY CONSUMER (herbivore, which eats the producer), then a SECONDARY CONSUMER (carnivore, which eats the primary consumer), and sometimes a TERTIARY CONSUMER at the top.

DECOMPOSERS (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste matter at every level, recycling nutrients back into the soil for producers to use again — without decomposers, nutrients would remain locked in dead matter indefinitely.

Energy flow through an ecosystem is one-directional and decreases at each successive trophic (feeding) level, because energy is lost as heat through respiration and other life processes at every stage — this is why food chains rarely extend beyond four or five links, and why there are always far more producers than top predators in a stable ecosystem.

Exam tip: distinguish "food chain" (a single, simple linear pathway) from "food web" (many interconnected food chains showing the more realistic, complex feeding relationships in a real ecosystem) — JAMB sometimes tests this distinction directly.
